description: How the personality cult, struggle sessions and propaganda turned the Cultural Revolution into total state penetration.
content_html:
The Mao Personality Cult

The personality cult around Mao Zedong reached its greatest intensity during the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), though its foundations had been laid throughout the 1950s. Lin Biao, head of the People's Liberation Army from 1959, was the cult’s chief architect. Lin oversaw the mass publication of the Little Red Book, organised the gigantic Tiananmen rallies of 1966, and required soldiers to read Mao’s writings as part of daily military routine. Mao badges — produced in the hundreds of millions — were worn by virtually every Chinese citizen. His portrait hung in every home, classroom, and workplace.

Key Fact

Lin Biao promoted the Mao cult more aggressively than anyone else in the leadership. Yet in September 1971, Lin was killed when his plane crashed in Mongolia. The official account said he had been attempting to flee after a failed coup plot against Mao. His death remains contested: it was a severe blow to the cult he had built, and Mao spent his final years increasingly isolated.

Propaganda and Thought Reform

Communist propaganda under Mao was pervasive and multi-layered. Newspapers, radio broadcasts, theatrical productions, and school lessons all transmitted the same ideological messages: class struggle, revolutionary heroism, selfless service to the collective, and absolute loyalty to Mao. The Party press did not report independently — it performed ideology.

Thought reform sessions were a central mechanism of control in workplaces, universities, and Party cells. Workers and students were required to attend regular meetings where they studied Mao’s texts, criticised their own thinking, and denounced colleagues. Refusing to participate, or appearing insufficiently enthusiastic, invited suspicion. These rituals bound together political loyalty and social conformity in daily life.

Tibet’s position within the PRC is a contested historical and political question. The PRC incorporated Tibet in 1950–51 through a combination of military force and the Seventeen Point Agreement. The PRC frames this as “peaceful liberation” from a feudal theocratic system that had kept Tibetans in poverty; Tibetan exile accounts and many Western scholars describe it as invasion and occupation that ended Tibetan political autonomy. In 1959, a Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule was suppressed; the Dalai Lama fled to India, where he established a government-in-exile. During the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), Red Guards destroyed hundreds of Tibetan monasteries, and religious practice was banned. The Jokhang Temple in Lhasa was used as a pigsty. The destruction of Tibetan religious and cultural heritage during this period is documented by both Chinese and international sources, though assessments of its scale and significance remain a point of dispute between the PRC government and Tibetan exile communities.

Dazhai as a Model of Communist Ideals

The Dazhai commune in Shanxi Province was central to propaganda during the Cultural Revolution and its aftermath. Its brigade leader Chen Yonggui was elevated to national hero status — a peasant who had supposedly transformed barren hillsides into productive terraces through collective effort and ideological commitment alone. The slogan “In Agriculture, Learn from Dazhai” was broadcast constantly. Chen became a vice-premier and appeared regularly alongside Mao and other leaders. Dazhai illustrates how the propaganda apparatus used individual cases — whether wholly or partly fabricated — to promote ideological messages about what revolutionary society could achieve.

Key Fact

Propaganda during the Cultural Revolution operated through multiple channels simultaneously: the personality cult (badges, portraits, rallies), the Party press, thought reform sessions in workplaces and schools, and model campaigns like Dazhai. Its aim was not merely to persuade but to make public displays of loyalty inescapable — creating a society where dissent had nowhere to hide.

The death of Lin Biao in September 1971 presented the CCP with a profound problem. Lin had been designated Mao’s chosen successor in the 1969 Party constitution. Now he was posthumously denounced as a traitor and counter-revolutionary. The regime that had elevated him found itself explaining why its propaganda had praised a man it now labelled a criminal. The “Criticise Lin Biao, Criticise Confucius” campaign that followed in 1973–74 attempted to redirect the political narrative, but many Chinese people drew private conclusions about the reliability of official propaganda more broadly. The incident illustrated the inherent instability of systems built on personal loyalty to a single leader.
exam_tip_html: Tibet is a politically sensitive topic that requires careful, balanced language. In your answer, state both the PRC framing (“peaceful liberation”) and the alternative view (invasion, occupation, destruction of autonomy) as held historical positions — not as one correct and one wrong answer. Examiners reward students who present contested topics with appropriate nuance. For questions about the personality cult, try to connect propaganda techniques to their political function: what was each technique designed to achieve and how effectively did it work?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Mao personality cult reached its height during the Cultural Revolution, driven largely by Lin Biao; it used badges, portraits, mass rallies, the Little Red Book, and thought reform sessions to make public displays of loyalty inescapable.
  • Tibet’s incorporation in 1950–51 and the destruction of its religious heritage during the Cultural Revolution are presented differently by the PRC (“liberation”) and by Tibetan exile and Western scholarship (“occupation”) — students must present both framings.
  • Lin Biao’s death in 1971 and subsequent denunciation as a traitor exposed the contradictions of a propaganda system built on personal loyalty, revealing the instability at the heart of the Mao cult.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Mao personality cult during the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A precise feature with specific supporting detail (e.g. mass publication of the Little Red Book, Tiananmen rallies, Mao badges). Secure: A relevant feature with basic supporting detail. Developing: A feature identified but without specific detail. Emerging: A vague or very limited statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Communist propaganda during the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct features with precise supporting detail (e.g. Party press, thought reform sessions, model campaigns). Secure: Two features, each with some detail. Developing: Two features but one or both lack evidence. Emerging: Only one feature or very limited information.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Mao personality cult was important to the success of the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons with specific evidence (e.g. how the cult gave Mao authority to override normal Party structures, role of Lin Biao, how it silenced potential opponents). Secure: Two reasons with supporting evidence. Developing: One well-developed reason or two thin points. Emerging: Simple statement with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Communist propaganda in maintaining CCP control during the Cultural Revolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of significance (immediate social control, long-term impact on intellectual life, how Lin Biao's death undermined it); counter-argument considered. Secure: Clear argument with evidence and some analysis. Developing: Relevant points with basic evidence; limited analysis of why significant. Emerging: Describes propaganda with minimal argument.

practice_questions.text: How far did the CCP successfully control the people of Tibet between 1950 and 1976? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing evidence of control (military incorporation, end of theocracy, Cultural Revolution destruction) against resistance (1959 uprising, Dalai Lama's exile, continued religious identity); both PRC and exile/Western framings acknowledged. Secure: Clear argument with evidence; some attempt to weigh extent of control. Developing: Mostly descriptive; limited weighing. Emerging: Simple narrative.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the death of Lin Biao in 1971 was damaging for the CCP's propaganda.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more developed reasons (Lin's role in building the cult, the contradiction of denouncing a praised leader, public loss of confidence in official claims). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two undeveloped points. Emerging: Basic statement.

knowledge_checks.q: Who was primarily responsible for building the Mao personality cult through mass publication of the Little Red Book?
What happened to the Dalai Lama following the 1959 Tibetan uprising?
options: He fled to India and established a government-in-exile
He signed a new agreement accepting CCP rule
He was persuaded to remain in Lhasa

knowledge_checks.q: Lin Biao died in _____ when his plane crashed in Mongolia, following an alleged coup attempt against Mao.
The model peasant _____ from Dazhai commune was elevated to national hero status and later became a vice-premier.
Match each concept to its correct description.
right: Commune held up as a propaganda model of revolutionary success
Elevation of Mao to near-divine status through propaganda
Mandatory study and self-criticism sessions in workplaces and schools

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the chief architect of the Mao personality cult?
When did Lin Biao die and what was the official explanation?
flashcard_questions.a: September 1971; alleged plane crash fleeing after failed coup

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Dalai Lama's response to the 1959 Tibetan uprising being suppressed?
flashcard_questions.a: Fled to India and established a government-in-exile
Mandatory study and self-criticism sessions requiring public display of loyalty
A Dazhai peasant brigade leader elevated to national hero and later vice-premier
Badges bearing Mao's portrait, worn by virtually every Chinese citizen

flashcard_questions.q: How did the PRC frame Tibet's incorporation in 1950–51?
flashcard_questions.a: As peaceful liberation from feudal theocracy

flashcard_questions.q: How do Tibetan exile accounts frame the same event?
flashcard_questions.a: As invasion ending Tibetan political autonomy

glossary_terms.definition: The elevation of a political leader to near-divine status through systematic propaganda involving images, slogans and rituals.
Mao's chosen political heir who promoted the Mao cult aggressively; died in a plane crash in 1971 after allegedly planning a coup.
State newspapers, notably the People's Daily, that transmitted official CCP ideological lines rather than independent reporting.
A process requiring individuals to internalise Communist ideology through mandatory study sessions, self-criticism and denunciations.
The spiritual and temporal leader of Tibetan Buddhism who fled to India following the failed 1959 uprising and established a government-in-exile.
A peasant brigade leader from Dazhai commune elevated to national hero status under Mao as evidence that revolutionary willpower overcame material obstacles.
